#6405. The 6 Best Metal Detectors for Treasure Hunters and Experts Alike

Find treasure on the beach (or at least a bunch of beer cans) with these top-of-the-line devices.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

You've probably seen a metal detectorist hard at work at a beach or park with their funky-looking gadget and thought, "I wish I had one of those." It's easy to fantasize about stumbling upon a hoard of buried pirate gold or, more realistically, a lost piece of jewelry, but the reality of metal detecting is this: It's more about the process of searching than the actual find itself.

That said, metal detecting can be a fun and relaxing hobby for anyone to try, especially with friends, and the barrier to entry is low. It’s an activity that gives you an excuse to spend a few hours outside, scouring the sand or dirt for coins or who-knows-what, and you might even find something that really makes it worth your while, though it's best if you don't expect to.

To determine the best metal detectors for newbies and experts alike, I tested a number of different models on the beaches and in the parks of South Florida, rating their performance, handling, and overall usability across several different terrains. I also consulted with an expert detectorist who helped me understand what factors to consider when making my choices. No matter which of these machines works best for your use case, all of them are great gets.

I selected the best metal detectors after trying a handful of options that came recommended to me by Jeff Lubbert, an expert detectorist who has been tracking down treasures and finding lost rings since the mid-1980s, and a handful of other expert detectorists.

Lubbert has used his metal detector in 28 states, one United States territory, five foreign countries, and three foreign territories, where he has recovered items adding up to approximately $980,000. He is president of the Eureka Treasure Hunters Club in Denver, Colorado, and has written articles about metal detectors for outlets like American Diggers. He's also appeared on the TV show Forensic Files.

To test accuracy, I buried an old spoon and two different coins—a quarter and a penny—8 inches underground to check their level of discrimination and pinpointing. I also used each detector for several hours in a variety of conditions, including in a grassy park and at the beach, in both dry sand and wet sand, and under several inches of surf.

The Minelab Vanquish 560 is a dynamic metal detector that works well on every terrain, including wet sand, and is incredibly intuitive to use. Unlike the slightly cheaper Vanquish 440, my previous top recommendation, the 560 is waterproof to 16 feet, which makes it suitable for wading and underwater use. It also includes a rechargeable battery, a flashlight, and Bluetooth headphone support, making it one of the most fully-featured detectors in this guide, and especially for this price.

While it only has four find modes (including an adjustable “custom” option). That’s are far fewer than you will find on professional-grade detectors like the Minelab Equinox 900, but it's still much more than enough for most amateur metal detectorists.

The Vanquish 560 punches well above its weight, and value-wise, it's the best detector we tested on a per-dollar basis. It may feel like a splurge for first-timers, but you’re getting what you pay for. And it’s an incredibly handsome upgrade for folks looking strong accuracy and some quality-of-life improvements.

Since I primarily spoke with experts and enthusiasts, the Nokta FindX Pro was not remotely on my radar when I first began my research. But it may just be the best option for new detectorists looking to dip a toe into the hobbyist pool. It’s an all-in-one kit, complete with an effective digging tool, a nice duffel bag, and decent headphones—all for less than $200.

While it is not as accurate as my other recommendations, it’s a more than capable VLF detector. I was able to find items at both parks and beaches, though I noticed that its performance really suffered on wet sand and underwater. Its compact frame and adjustable handle make it accommodating to a wider-than-average range of newcomers, including kids and adults.

If you’re interested in the hobby and don’t want to spend too much to try it, the FindX Pro is a great fit for beginners.

While I wasn’t able to get this detector in for my current round of tests, Lubbert recommended the Minelab Manticore for expert detectorists who want the ultimate metal detector experience. He says it can visualize the ground beneath it in a 2D map, directing you to finds with depths and ID targets. It should work well in any terrain, including underwater, and has the most advanced backlight of any Minelab machine. Plus, with 10 search modes, there are many options for veteran detectorists looking to optimize for a specific type of search.

The price is substantial, but if you’re willing to spend this much money on a detector, I’m confident that it will be worth it.

The Simplex line is often recommended by experts as a good entry point for new detectorists. Nokta is one of the two biggest brands in the metal detecting game—the other is Minelab—and the Simplex Lite is a strong, basic VLF detector. I found it had top-notch discrimination, plenty of find modes, and a good coil size that easily found my testing materials and led me to beer cans, aluminum foil, and plenty of other objects on the beach.

Because this is a single-frequency VLF detector, it doesn’t perform as well as the Vanquish 440, especially on the mineralized sand at saltwater beaches. It’s still a very capable machine, though—even more so if you’re searching for a specific type of item, particularly coins and jewelry. Though it offers fewer customization options than its more expensive multi-frequency counterparts, it’s also much easier to pick up and use as a newcomer.

For those who are looking to spend a bit more, you can upgrade to the Simplex Ultra, which adds Bluetooth support and gives you precision detector tools like target ID scale and depth.

Underwater metal detecting is typically the domain of serious enthusiasts, especially if it’s in seawater. If this sounds intriguing, two different experts for metal detector recommendations (including Lubbert) suggest the XP Deus II, a high-end machine that specializes in just that. Expert Stanley Ross, known as the Metal Detector Man, who we spoke with for this article previously, says that he uses his Deus II to search for lost rings and other jewelry on the beach all the time.

The Deus II has something called "fast multi-frequency" technology, which allows for superior multi-frequency detection in a variety of conditions, and it's rated for up to 20 meters of water, a massive upgrade compared to our other picks that top out at 5 meters of water resistance. Our other multi-frequency picks use similar technology, but the Deus II offers better and faster response in saltwater conditions, making it easier to pinpoint buried targets without having to pass over the same spot multiple times, especially underwater.In order to use the Deus II underwater, however, you'll need a few accessories, including its waterproof wireless headphones and an underwater remote control. While these upgrades are technically “optional” in the sense that you can easily use the Deus II on land without them, they are virtually required for anything beyond getting your ankles wet.

Both of these additions will increase the price of the overall package considerably, depending on which exact model of headphones you choose. Both the $280 WS6 headphones (which can control the detector, but are not recommended for underwater use) and the $749 remote control have slightly different interfaces, but the remote control is generally recommended for both ease of use and underwater functionality. Because of its high customizability and 12 preset modes, the Deus II isn't quite as beginner-friendly as some of our other picks.

While I haven't yet tested the Deus II for myself, it’s highly regarded among enthusiasts. If you're interested in underwater detecting—whether that's wading around or even diving down—this choice will not disappoint.

The Minelab Equinox 900 is the most feature-rich metal detector I tested. From the second I picked it up, I could tell that it would be a cut above the rest. The build quality is noticeably better than that of other, less expensive models I tested—it just feels more substantial.

Its features and performance back up that first impression. The Equinox 900 consistently performed better than its less expensive counterparts as well, pinpointing targets precisely and identifying both their depth and target ID. Though I was able to find my planted targets with every detector, the Equinox 900 directed me precisely to all three, making the process quicker and easier in both dry and wet sand.

It also features a number of settings and tools that improve the detecting experience, including six customizable frequency settings, an easy-adjust handle, and Bluetooth support so you can use wireless headphones. All that customization is incredible if you’re an expert. I personally had more success using the premade settings, but I can see detectorists like Lubbert fine-tuning searches to great effect.

I was especially taken with its handgrip vibration feature, which gives you a rumbling haptic response when the Equinox picks up a target. It’s a great way to get your attention in a loud area, if you’re hearing-impaired, or if you’re just on a long walk and not paying close attention. Personally, I found it very helpful while roaming some very popular stretches of Miami’s beaches.

It’s worth noting that Minelab lists the Equinox 900 as a bit heavier than the other models we tested, though I personally didn’t notice a difference, even after several hours of sweeping. At more than triple the price of my best overall pick, it’s fair to say that the Equinox 900 is an investment for serious hobbyists. But it is far and away the most effective choice I tested and a worthy upgrade.

In addition to a decent pair of headphones, it helps to carry a pinpointer when using your metal detector. These precise, short-range auxiliary detectors assist you with determining the exact location of a find after picking something up with your detector’s large coil.

This one, from Minelab, is relatively expensive, but fully waterproof with five sensitivity levels, and it works very well. It also features ferrous discrimination, which allows it to tell if a target is made of ferrous metals like iron or non-ferrous metals like gold, silver, or copper. It isn’t strictly necessary but is an extra feature you’ll enjoy using in trash-filled parks.

We tested and loved the Minelab Vanquish 440, a slightly cheaper version of our current best overall pick, the Vanquish 560. It was recently replaced with a new and improved model, the Minelab Vanquish 460, which is also a strong choice. We ultimately chose to recommend the 560 because it offers a more robust set of features and works well over more types of terrain.

While shopping for a metal detector, you need to take into account a number of key factors, particularly the type, coil size, weight, and extra features like backlight and frequency customization. Weight and build quality also make a big difference, especially when you use these devices for hours at a time. It was initially hard to weigh these distinct traits, but after testing these machines myself, the features worth springing for became clear.

If you’re going to shop for a hobby-grade metal detector, it’s important to understand how they work. This is fairly technical equipment, so manufacturers will cater their products primarily to veterans who already have a bit of knowledge, which may be intimidating to new people.

Most metal detectors have a round head called the “search coil,” which is the actual detector itself. It has two parts, the transmitter coil and the receiver coil, which work in tandem to produce an electromagnetic field that shoots down into the ground wherever you wave it. When the field hits metal, it triggers another magnetic effect in response, which the coil picks up. Depending on the device, that signal may be able to tell you how deep an object is buried, based on the strength of the response.

Most of the detectors I recommend can determine what kind of metal they’re reading by measuring the object’s “phase shift,” or the time it takes for the object to react when the coil changes its magnetic current. This function, called “discrimination,” can sometimes help you figure out if your quarry is worth digging up before you go to the trouble of getting your digging tools out. However, as Lubbert notes, discrimination is not always reliable, and it’s generally best to err on the side of digging if you think you’ve found something worthwhile.

The first thing to look at before buying a metal detector is where you plan to use it, as some detectors are better equipped to scan specific types of terrain. For example, if you live near the coast and plan to sweep your local beach, you may want a different model than someone looking under hard soil in local parks. Though there are many kinds of detectors, I focused on the two most frequently used by novices and veteran hobbyists.

The physical size of the metal detector coil is important, too. If you don’t sweep the coil over an object, you aren’t going to get a ping, so bigger is better. Under most conditions, Lubbert recommends looking for a coil that’s at least 11 inches in diameter.

That said, Lubbert advises that smaller coils have their uses, especially in wooded areas, since it’s easier to get between twigs, grass, and weeds with a more compact head. Larger coils can theoretically detect objects that are deeper underground, but they’re also more susceptible to electromagnetic interference from the environment. He recommends having both a compact coil and a large coil option if you plan to scan a wide range of environments.

In general, all of my recommendations here seem relatively light on paper—the heaviest weighs only a few pounds. Keep in mind, though, that you could be waving this device around with one arm for hours at a time. Even a few ounces can greatly impact how quickly you tire out.

Mid-range and high-end metal detectors tend to feature backlit displays, which come in handy when searching in low-light conditions. (Some high-end models even come with flashlight functions). Though not a universal feature, I consider this essential for all but the cheapest options.

High-end metal detectors grant you a degree of customization through advanced settings, allowing you to set a specific level of discrimination that, when properly used, can help you identify relics and coins in a variety of environments. You need to know what you’re doing to take full advantage of these do-it-yourself search modes, but there are guides online to help you learn as you go.

Lastly, most metal detectors I researched and/or tested feature built-in batteries that last for hours on a full charge. That said, some models—including one of my picks—use disposable batteries instead. There are advantages and disadvantages to both: Disposable batteries can be replaced quickly, but you need to keep spare cells on you. It comes down to your preference, so go with what feels right.

“Make each swing of the detector take about 2 seconds and overlap your swings so that the coil covers all of the ground,” Lubbert says. “Wear headphones, as it helps you hear those deep target whispers.”

Lubbert also said that detectorists should be happy with what they find, and that you should expect 95 percent of your digs to result in trash. When that happens, be cool, and make sure to dispose of it properly.

According to Lubbert, a dedicated detectorist should have a pinpointer, proper recovery tools like a shovel, and a pouch to store trash and treasure separately.

Based on my testing experience and to echo his point above, I found headphones to be a must-have when using a metal detector, as the built-in speakers are difficult to hear, especially on a crowded beach.

Finding a legal place to use your metal detector is not as easy as you might think. It’s illegal to use a detector in U.S. National Parks and historic battlefields. Many cities ban using them on public property or require you to apply for a permit beforehand. Make sure to check your local city and county laws to determine if and where you may be allowed to use a metal detector and if you’ll need a permit to do so.

And, of course, if you plan to use your detector on private property, you should obtain permission from the owner, or else you might dig up a lawsuit instead of treasure.

Steven T. Wright is a freelance writer based in Miami, FL. He has been a full-time writer of various things for around a decade, especially long-form features about tech and digital culture. New research shows that a powerful 2021 marsquake emanating from Valles Marineris — the largest canyon in the solar system — was triggered by unexpected movement in a fault line deep below the gigantic structure, revealing that tectonic activity can still occur on geologically "dead" worlds.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Mars' supersize Valles Marineris — the largest known canyon in the solar system — is still tectonically active even though the Red Planet is geologically "dead," new research on a previously record-breaking marsquake reveals.

On Aug. 25, 2021, NASA's InSight lander, which touched down on the Red Planet in 2018, detected a powerful marsquake, designated S0976a. The Martian equivalent of an earthquake reached magnitude 4.2, which, at the time, was the most powerful quake that InSight or any other Mars lander had ever seen. (Since then, a 4.7 magnitude marsquake in May 2022 knocked it off the top spot, but S0976a remains second on this list.)

Unlike most marsquakes, which have been minor tremors triggered by meteorite impacts near InSight, S0976a was a deep rumble that originated from the opposite side of Mars as the robotic seismologist, in the western half of Valles Marineris.

In the new study, published Oct. 15 in the journal Nature Communications, researchers reanalyzed the seismic wave data of S0976a and found that the quake originated from within a fault line running below the enormous canyon. The most likely explanation, they argue, is that there was tectonic movement in this hidden crustal crack.

"Valles Marineris is one of the most spectacular geological structures anywhere in the solar system, but until now we didn't know for certain that its faults are still active," study first author Jung-Hun Song, a researcher in the Department of Earth Science and Engineering at Imperial College London, said in a statement. "What we see is that this is not just a 'dead' fossil landscape, as faults deep beneath the canyon can still slip and generate marsquakes, long after the geological processes that originally formed them have ceased."

S0976a is the second-largest marsquake ever detected by NASA's InSight lander, shown here in a NASA clean room on April 30, 2015.

Valles Marineris is an enormous set of interconnected gullies and ravines stretching up to 2,500 miles (4,000 kilometers) in length, or roughly 10 times longer than the Grand Canyon. It is also up to 20 times wider and five times deeper, meaning that if you found yourself stranded at the bottom, it could take you a couple of months to climb out again.

The enormous chasm — named after the Mariner 9 spacecraft, which helped discover it in 1971 — is clearly visible from space, like a giant scar carved into the Red Planet's face. From orbit, you would also see the nearby Tharsis region, which is home to Mars' giant volcanoes, including Olympus Mons, which is at least three times taller than Mount Everest.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

These imposing structures are proof that Mars was once geologically active, perhaps even more so than Earth. However, scientists think the Red Planet's surface has remained relatively unchanged for nearly 3 billion years, according to the European Space Agency.

Valles Marineris is almost as long as the continental U.S. is wide. (In this photo, captured by NASA's Mars Odyssey orbiter, an optical illusion known as relief inversion may make the canyon appear as if it is raised above the surface, which it is not.)

The reason for this is twofold. First, Mars is smaller than Earth, so its core and mantle have cooled much faster than our planet's and are, therefore, less dynamic. Second, Mars has no tectonic plates. Instead of giant patches of crust butting against each other, the Red Planet's outermost layer is almost completely intact and acts like a giant lid over its cooling molten innards. (Research published earlier this week throws the "dead" theory into question, hinting that magma may still lurk below dormant Martian volcanoes).

Despite this, Mars still has fault lines. But rather than being a boundary between tectonic plates, these lines are more like giant cracks in its crust, some of which are visible at the surface.

In the new study, researchers discovered proof of what they call a slip-strike marsquake, where "blocks of crust move horizontally past one another along a steep, deeply rooted fault," the team said. They believe this occurred somewhere between 12 and 25 miles (20 to 40 km) below Valles Marineris.

The researchers also simulated several other potential causes of the marsquake, including a major asteroid strike or a landslide within the canyon, but nothing else could explain the patterns they saw.

Using seismic wave data captured by InSight, researchers were able to pinpoint the epicenter of the S0976a masquake (represented as a yellow star near the top of this map).

"What makes the result compelling is that several completely different types of evidence point in the same direction," Song said.

The finding also raises hopes that similar tectonic activity could one day be detected on other worlds across the solar system.

"Our study opens up exciting possibilities for discovering ongoing seismic activity on other planetary bodies that we might otherwise consider geologically inactive," Song said.

The discovery highlights the importance of detecting and studying marsquakes, which were only officially discovered in 2019, thanks to InSight. (Scientists have since uncovered older marsquakes, using data collected by the Viking landers in the late 1970s.)

InSight sent back a final selfie to Earth on Dec. 19, 2022, showing a heavy coating of Martian dust on its solar panels. Its mission was officially ended two days later.

"S0976a has turned out to be an extraordinary event," study co-author Doyeon Kim, head of Imperial College London's Terrestrial and Planetary Seismology Lab, said in the statement. "Its waves traveled through the core and helped us investigate the deepest part of Mars, and now they are telling us what happened at the source itself. From a single marsquake, we can learn both about the center of the planet and about an active fault beneath one of its most remarkable landscapes."

Scientists have similarly used marsquake vibrations from InSight to map out Mars' interior, leading to several intriguing subsurface discoveries, including dozens of blobs left over from ancient protoplanets, the hidden cause of the planet's uneven hemispheres, a potentially active "mantle plume" and a gigantic underground water reservoir containing enough liquid to cover Mars with a mile-deep (1.6 km) ocean.

Unfortunately, in December 2022, InSight quite literally bit the dust: A thick covering of Martian powder blocked its solar panels, preventing the lander from returning signals to Earth and thus ending its mission.

This means we currently have no way of detecting new marsquakes. However, the new study proves that the lander's archived data can still lead to exciting discoveries.

Song, J., Kim, D., Kolawole, F., Davis, J. M., Parry, R., & Maguire, R. (2026). Active crustal straining and fault reactivation at Valles Marineris. Nature Communications, 17(1). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-026-78193-6

Extra financial support during pregnancy and after birth can help more babies thrive in their earliest days.

The Rx Kids program in Flint, Mich., launched in January 2024, provides extra cash to pregnant residents and their infants, unconditionally. Researchers compared neonatal deaths — those in the first four weeks of life — in 2025 with those in 2021 through 2024 in Flint. The city’s neonatal mortality rate dropped from 10 deaths per 1,000 live births to 5 deaths per 1,000 live births, researchers report November 2 in JAMA Pediatrics. The early neonatal mortality rate, covering deaths in the first week of life, fell from 8 per 1,000 to 2. For the rest of Michigan, rates were stable over the study’s time period.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

“As a pediatrician, there is no outcome more important than babies surviving,” says Mona Hanna of the Michigan State University College of Human Medicine in Flint, who is also the founder and director of Rx Kids. “These early findings suggest that something as simple as providing families with financial support during pregnancy and infancy may help save babies’ lives.”

Income tends to drop and expenses rise in the months before and after a birth, making the perinatal period especially difficult financially for many families. Economic precarity can expose moms and babies to health harms. For example, housing instability and homelessness is associated with preterm birth and low birth weight.

Backed by public and private funds, Rx Kids got started in Flint, a city with a high rate of child poverty that has been dealing with the public health fallout of lead contamination in the water distribution system. Nearly 100 percent of the community participates in the program. Flint families receive $1,500 once during pregnancy and $500 per month in the baby’s first year. Anyone who is a resident, at least 16 weeks pregnant or with a newborn up to six months old can enroll. Families have put the extra cash toward diapers, transportation, housing and safe places for their babies to sleep, Hanna says.

“Every day, we hear from moms who tell us, ‘I can breathe’ or ‘A weight has been lifted off my shoulders.’ They tell us they feel less stressed, more hopeful, more supported and more loved,” Hanna says.

The support has had a measurable health impact, with studies linking the program to more access to prenatal care, a decrease in the preterm birth rate and in low-weight births and fewer neonatal intensive care admissions.

Rx Kids has now expanded to dozens of communities in Michigan and Ohio.

Using machine learning, astronomers developed a new way of looking at James Webb telescope data that allows far-off planets to emerge from their stars' glare.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

When it comes to spotting planets orbiting distant stars, the biggest hurdle is often separating the signal from the noise — specifically, trying to distinguish a planet from the stellar glare around it. That's true even for the most sophisticated telescopes, including the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST).

Now, astronomers have developed a new way to spot planets that were formerly drowned out in a sea of light. Using a combination of modeling and machine learning techniques, they picked out a previously hidden giant exoplanet in data from JWST. The results were published Nov. 4 in the journal Nature.

"Planets are a million times fainter than their stars," study first author Rodrigo Ferrer-Chavez, an astronomer at Northwestern University, said in a statement. "So, to image exoplanets, we need to remove that glare."

Telescopes like JWST use instruments called coronagraphs to block out some of this excess light, similar to the way the moon and a pinhole camera operate during a total solar eclipse. But even the best coronagraphs have limitations — for example, they can't block all the glare, and the telescopes themselves move.

Even the most stable telescopes vibrate almost imperceptibly as they collect light, so the images a telescope produces contain ever-so-slight mismatches compared with what the instrument actually sees. These slight shifts can be enough to obscure even very large exoplanets.

To address this, Ferrer-Chavez and his team developed a "digital twin" of JWST that virtually recreates how light travels through the telescope's detectors, minus any movement-based imperfections. To fine-tune this digital replica, the researchers used computational models based in real-world physics alongside machine learning techniques similar to those used to train AI. But the authors stressed that this is not an AI model.

"Because we already know the physics, we don't need AI to understand what's happening," study co-author Jason Wang, also an astrophysicist at Northwestern, said in a statement.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

The researchers named their approach Physics-based Learning for Imaging Planets, or FLIP.

Using FLIP, the team analyzed data from three stars, including 51 Eridani, which is located around 97 light-years from Earth and was already suspected to have a giant exoplanet orbiting it. Although the planet, called 51 Eridani b, had been detected by ground-based telescopes, it was drowned out by light in previous JWST observations. With FLIP, however, 51 Eridani b popped out from the dataset.

The scientists hope this approach will help astronomers pick out even more hard-to-spot exoplanets, especially ones that look like the planets in our own backyard. In the nearly 35-year history of exoplanet hunting, the vast majority of planets we've found have been radically different from those in our own solar system, partially because larger and more reflective worlds are easier to spot with current telescopes.

"It's not that [solar-system-like planets] don't exist," Ferrer-Chavez said. "It's that we can't see them."

#6398. Scientists tracked millions of phones to uncover patterns in carbon emissions

Scientists used anonymized cell phone mobility data to estimate carbon emissions, testing the approach across four countries.

When COVID-19 lockdowns froze the planet in early 2020, carbon emissions plummeted almost overnight.

The problem? The instruments tracking those emissions couldn’t keep up.

Conventional inventories lag reality by months. Satellite inversions come with their own trade-offs between resolution and coverage.

A new study explores another approach: using people’s movements to help estimate carbon emissions.

The research was led by Mengning Wang and Xin Lu from China’s National University of Defense Technology.

Collaborators included Xiaoling Zhang from the University of Hong Kong and scholars from various international institutions.

The researchers turned anonymized cell phone signals from 318 million Chinese mobile users into what amounts to a near-real-time carbon meter.

They tested the framework across four countries.

Commuting, deliveries, business trips, and holiday travel often generate carbon emissions.

The researchers reasoned that if so many carbon-producing processes involve physically moving people and goods, then the movement itself might serve as a fast measuring stick.

They took anonymized signaling data from China Unicom and converted it into daily intercity mobility networks.

Each city became a node and each flow of people between cities became an edge.

From these networks they extracted structural features – how central a city is, how tightly clustered its connections are, how many links it maintains – and combined those with population and geographic data.

Then they trained machine learning models against the GRACED dataset, which tracks daily CO2 emissions across seven sectors: power, industry, residential consumption, ground transport, domestic aviation, international aviation, and shipping.

The window researchers studied was January and February 2020. It’s hard to imagine a harder test.

Spring Festival travel sent 68.74 million daily intercity trips surging through the network. Then lockdowns hit.

Mobility crashed by 71.3%. Multi-source carbon emissions dropped from an average of roughly 356.5 million kilograms of carbon per day to a minimum of 209.6 million – a 41.2% collapse. The whole thing happened in weeks.

And yet the correlation between daily national mobility and CO2 emissions held firm at r = 0.89. At the city level, it was a more modest but still significant r = 0.49.

The best-performing model – LightGBM, a tree-based ensemble – achieved R² values of 1.00 for multi-source emissions, 0.99 for domestic aviation, and 0.98 for ground transportation across 366 cities and 60 days.

Those are extraordinary numbers for something as messy as urban carbon output.

The real surprise came when the framework crossed borders.

Using open-source mobility datasets, the team applied the same approach to Italy, the continental United States, and Mexico.

The model reached R² values of 0.91, 0.95, and 0.99 respectively against the GRACED inventory.

Tested against a completely independent dataset – ODIAC, which derives emissions from nighttime light imagery and power-plant data at 1 km resolution – it still scored between 0.90 and 0.99.

Four countries, two independent benchmarks, consistent accuracy.

Something unexpected emerged from the mobility data. The Louvain community detection algorithm carved China’s 366 cities into 11 functional clusters.

These are groupings defined not by provincial borders but by how people actually move between them. Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei formed one cluster, pumping out 62.75 million kilograms of carbon daily.

The Yangtze River Delta formed another, at 49.71 million.

These clusters aren’t just descriptive. More central, more connected clusters emit more carbon.

But here’s the policy hook. China’s existing climate governance tends to target a handful of major emitting cities while overlooking smaller ones that sit in structurally critical positions within the network.

The mobility-defined clusters offer something different: a template for coordinated regional decarbonization that matches how economies actually function rather than how administrative maps happen to be drawn.

The authors aren’t overselling this. They call mobility a “partial but observable proxy” – a complement to inventories, not a replacement.

The Chinese analysis covers a single extraordinary two-month window. The data captures intercity movement, not what happens within a city.

Mobility alone may not fully capture emissions changes driven by seasonal energy demand, holiday schedules, or weekly cycles.

There are subtler problems too. Cellular signaling data inherits all the biases of telecom coverage – regional disparities, operator market share, sampling artifacts.

And the fundamental link between mobility and emissions could shift as remote work spreads, transport electrifies, and travel patterns reshape.

A correlation forged during the most dramatic behavioral disruption in modern history might not hold the same way during a quiet Tuesday in 2030.

Still, the core appeal is hard to argue with. Standard emissions inventories are accurate but glacially slow.

With timely access to mobility data, the framework could provide frequently updated emissions estimates.

If it scales, climate policymakers would gain a behavior-informed reading of the present rather than a months-old accounting of the past.

The team calls for fusing their mobility approach with remote sensing, energy structure data, and meteorological variables.

The ambition is to make carbon monitoring something closer to weather forecasting: imperfect, always updating, but fast enough to actually be useful.

The study is published in the journal The Innovation.

#6397. A drug-free diabetes treatment? An implant lowers blood sugar in mice

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The device banishes extra blood glucose by converting it to a compound excreted in urine

Excess blood glucose (shown in white in this illustration) is the target of a new experimental device. In mice, the sugar gets converted into a compound which the kidneys can excrete in urine.

NEMES LASZLO/SCIENCE PHOTO LIBRARY/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A wireless implant that clears excess sugar from the blood could someday offer a drug-free way to treat type 2 diabetes and obesity.

In mice with both conditions, the under-the-skin device brought high blood sugar back to normal within 60 to 90 minutes of being switched on, researchers report October 22 in Science. After six weeks, the treated mice lost up to 10 percent of their body weight and had lower triglycerides, a type of fat in the blood.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Diabetes affects about 830 million people worldwide. Conventional type 2 diabetes treatments like insulin and GLP-1 drugs require careful dosing. Even experimental diabetes-controlling implants still rely on the hormone insulin, which clears sugar from the bloodstream but doesn’t rid the body of it, says Martin Fussenegger, a bioengineer at ETH Zurich. The new implant instead removes glucose from the body without added drugs, genes or living cells.

The 3-centimeter-long device contains a catalyst made of gold flakes and platinum particles on spongelike graphite. When electricity powers it, the catalyst converts glucose into gluconate, a compound that is easier for the kidneys to flush out in urine. With less glucose available for energy, the body may turn to its fat stores instead, Fussenegger and colleagues suspect. In mice, that shift showed up as higher blood levels of chemicals released when fat breaks down, such as ketones. “This system kind of targets the root cause, which is the energy surplus by glucose in the body,” Fussenegger says.

The implant works like an automatic sugar-removal system: A wearable glucose monitor detects high blood sugar levels and sends readings through a smartphone that switches the implant on. When levels return to a safer range, it switches off. The automated system ran for two weeks in eight mice. The catalyst itself remained able to convert glucose after up to three months under their skin, though the study didn’t establish how long the entire device would last.

And it’s still unknown how well the device would work in people. “This is a potentially promising method,” says David Klonoff, an endocrinologist at Sutter Mills-Peninsula Medical Center in Burlingame, Calif., who was not involved in the study. “But the risks are significant and must be carefully ruled out before it can be safely tested on humans.”

Researchers need to determine how much gluconate the kidneys can clear, Klonoff says. If it builds up, it could disrupt the body’s acid-base balance, causing symptoms such as nausea or confusion; excreting it could also deplete electrolytes such as sodium and potassium, he notes.

Scaling up the device is another challenge. Humans consume about 250 grams of carbohydrates daily, compared with two grams for mice, Klonoff estimates. Meeting that demand could require a much larger implant or multiple devices, he says. In a lab test, a larger device cleared nearly all glucose from about 5 liters of solution, roughly an adult’s blood volume, though not a full day’s glucose intake.

Fussenegger’s team plans to test the device in pigs and sheep before considering human trials. If proven safe and effective, it could offer an alternative to existing diabetes treatments and a new weight-loss option for people regardless of whether they have diabetes, he says.

#6396. Webb reveals the hidden activity inside a turbulent stellar nursery

Webb peers through thick cosmic dust in NGC 7129, revealing hidden young stars, protostars, glowing gas, and powerful outflows.

Today’s Image of the Day from the European Space Agency reveals a stellar nursery where young stars are changing the clouds that gave birth to them.

The James Webb Space Telescope captured NGC 7129, a star-forming region about 3,300 light-years from Earth.

Thick clouds of gas and dust obscure much of the activity at visible wavelengths.

Webb’s infrared vision can penetrate that material, bringing previously hidden stars and structures into view.

The result shows much more than a collection of newborn stars. NGC 7129 contains objects at several stages of early stellar development.

Some are still gathering material. Others have moved closer to the long, stable period of life that includes stars such as our Sun.

Stars do not all mature at the same rate. More massive stars generally form and evolve faster than smaller ones.

That difference allows astronomers to study several chapters of stellar development within the same region.

The brightest central star in this scene is LkH(alpha) 234. It has about five to eight times the mass of the Sun and produces the image’s most noticeable diffraction pattern.

It is a pre-main-sequence star, meaning it has largely finished collecting mass but has not yet begun the sustained hydrogen fusion that will define its main-sequence life.

At this stage, gravity continues to pull the star inward. As it contracts, its interior grows hotter.

Eventually, conditions in the core will become intense enough for hydrogen fusion to begin.

This transition matters because a young star does not develop quietly.

Even before reaching the main sequence, it can send powerful streams of material into the gas around it.

Those outflows can reshape a stellar nursery across surprisingly large distances.

The clearest evidence appears to the left of LkH(alpha) 234. A golden cavity stretches roughly 3.5 light-years across.

Outflows produced during an earlier stage of the star’s development carved into the surrounding molecular cloud, which consists largely of hydrogen.

Radiation and outflowing material from the star energize the gas and make it glow.

Some gas gets swept away, but the process does not simply shut down star formation.

Other material becomes compressed. Dense pockets can then provide the conditions needed for additional stars to develop.

Several young stars are visible inside the cavity. Some are also pre-main-sequence stars, and they produce stellar winds of their own.

As these winds push into surrounding gas, they create curved structures called bow shocks.

The stars also create a hot environment beside colder, denser molecular material. The boundary between these environments is known as a photodissociation region.

Energetic radiation breaks hydrogen molecules apart into individual atoms there.

The process changes the chemistry, heating and cooling of the cloud and helps determine how it evolves.

Molecular clouds are the raw material for star formation, but the stars born inside them gradually help destroy them.

Radiation, winds, and outflows can disperse gas or alter its chemistry.

Over millions of years, those effects can erode the cloud and change where new stars are able to form.

NGC 7129 gives astronomers a particularly useful view of that process because its stars have reached different developmental stages.

Their combined activity shows how star formation can both disrupt a cloud and compress parts of it into conditions favorable for further stellar growth.

The right side of Webb’s image tells an earlier part of the story.

Clumpy red material conceals protostars that are younger than the pre-main-sequence stars visible elsewhere in the region.

Protostars form after cold molecular gas and dust collapse and fragment into dense concentrations.

They continue gaining mass from surrounding material.

At the same time, they can eject narrow, extremely hot outflows that slam into the dense matter around them.

Those collisions produce shocks within the gray material surrounding the protostars.

They help create the textured appearance seen by Webb and contribute to the region’s red glow.

Several protostars are active at once, so their outflows overlap from Earth’s viewpoint. That makes this side of NGC 7129 look especially tangled.

Yet the apparent disorder contains valuable information about stars that would otherwise remain hidden behind dust.

Infrared observations give astronomers access to these deeply embedded objects before they emerge from their birth clouds.

In NGC 7129, Webb captures stars at different points along that path while also revealing how strongly they affect their surroundings.

The nursery will continue changing as its young stars mature.

Gas will disperse, dense pockets may collapse, and some newly formed stars will eventually settle into the hydrogen-fusing stage that powers the Sun today.

About half of people with long COVID see meaningful improvement in their symptoms after three years, a new study found.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Symptoms of long COVID ease in half of patients within three years of the infection that kicked off their illness.

That's the primary conclusion of a new study that tracked over 1,000 patients with long COVID, a chronic condition that can emerge after an infection with the SARS-CoV-2 virus. Among the patients, the chance of improvement varied sharply depending on how the condition affected their bodily systems.

In the study, published Tuesday (Nov. 3) in the journal Annals of Internal Medicine, roughly 60% of patients whose predominant symptoms were changes to their ability to taste or smell had significantly improved three years after their first positive test. But less than 20% of those with a multisystem presentation had improved in that time frame.

This latter group had symptoms that affected their cardiac, nervous and gastrointestinal systems, among others. An expert told Live Science that the condition resembled myalgic encephalomyelitis/chronic fatigue syndrome (ME/CFS), which often arises after an infection and similarly impacts a wide range of bodily systems.

The new study's findings could help direct the structure of future clinical trials of treatments for long COVID, experts said.

The patients in the study were enrolled in the long-term RECOVER Adult Study. Funded by the National Institutes of Health, the project has recruited thousands of adults across the United States who previously tested positive for COVID-19.

Researchers scored patients based on how they were affected by a range of symptoms, including fatigue, brain fog, shortness of breath and heart palpitations. The study included patients who scored more than 10 points on a 30-point scale — called the 2024 LC Research Index (LCRI) — which attempted to capture these different symptom combinations.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Nearly 1,020 patients met this requirement and were tracked over time; they had in-person appointments and filled out symptom surveys every three months. Scientists marked patients as "improved" once they recorded LCRI scores of 10 or less at two consecutive visits. They found that 36% of the participants had improved two years after their inciting COVID-19 infection, and that figure rose to 50% after three years.

LCRIs hit zero for 26% of the participants after three years, meaning all of their symptoms were gone at the time of the survey.

Reeder said he was careful to avoid describing the participants as "recovered." This decision was influenced by input from the long COVID community to the RECOVER Adult Study, he said. They highlighted that their symptoms can wax and wane, whereas "recovery" implies a permanent resolution. The new study didn't capture, for example, whether individual patients who recorded meaningful improvement later relapsed.

The researchers analyzed which SARS-CoV-2 strain was associated with the most long COVID cases, controlling for patient vaccination status.

Some patients' journeys were far less straightforward than the top-line data might suggest. Although men and women improved at similar rates, adults under 46 were more likely to improve than older participants were. Patients affected by the Omicron variants of SARS-CoV-2, which emerged in 2021 and quickly became the dominant strain of the virus, were more likely to improve than those infected with earlier strains.

Some of the starkest differences in improvement rates were seen between patients with different symptoms.

In a previous study, RECOVER researchers had grouped participants into five subtypes, using an algorithm to connect patients with similar predominant symptoms:

In the new study, patients in the last three groups were less likely to get better within three years. The final group's rate was particularly low, at just 19%.

Dr. Carmen Scheibenbogen, an immunologist at Charité University Medicine Berlin, said these patients' progress resembles that of people with ME/CFS.

"It looks as if at least a major subgroup is suffering from ME-CFS," Scheibenbogen said, noting that COVID-19 may have triggered their condition. "This is a disease which is triggered by different infections, but in the end, the disease [itself] is very similar," she said.

Like long COVID, ME/CFS can affect a wide array of bodily systems, and it remains poorly understood despite recent advances in research.

The team's new findings highlight the need for clinical trials to test possible treatments for long COVID. Both Scheibenbogen and study co-author Harrison Reeder, a biostatistician at Massachusetts General Hospital, said these subtypes would be important to consider in the design of these potential trials.

The multisystem subgroup, Reeder said, "might be a group where an effective intervention can make a bigger difference than people who stand to potentially have a higher chance of improvement regardless."

Future work would need to further scientists' understanding of people affected by long COVID at the level of their genes and proteins, both scientists said.

"There's a lot of work to do in RECOVER and in the world of long COVID research," Harrison said. "There's a lot of opportunity."

#6393. MIT researchers built a tiny new computer from squishy materials that works like a human brain

A soft film 2 nanometers thick lets a tiny device hold a memory for seconds and then fire like a neuron, all within one part.

Computers left moving parts behind a long time ago, trading gears and wheels for electrons flowing through chips that don’t change shape.

At a size far smaller than a single brain cell, a new device goes back to motion. Once squeezed, it takes a few seconds to recover its shape, so it can add up signals and fire, like an artificial neuron.

Because of that delay, one tiny part holds a short memory and acts on it. That job usually takes extra components such as capacitors.

Farnaz Niroui, an associate professor in MIT’s Department of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (EECS) and a member of its Research Laboratory of Electronics (RLE), led the team that built it. Chemist Jeremiah Johnson of MIT’s Department of Chemistry joined them.

It’s a laboratory demonstration, and its biggest energy savings are a projection rather than a measurement.

Part of the inspiration came from animals that handle information where it arrives. For example, many of an octopus’s nerve cells are in its arms, which can sense and respond without waiting on the brain.

“You can think of an octopus as continuous computing matter, with computing, memory, sensing, and actuation distributed throughout its body,” Niroui said.

Mechanical computing goes back at least to the gears of the ancient Antikythera mechanism.

Modern mechanical computers have mostly stayed at the scale of millimeters. Shrinking them further runs into a basic problem. Surfaces brought within a few billionths of a meter of each other pull together and stick.

To get around it, the researchers laid a soft polymer film called PDMS, about 2 nanometers thick, between two gold electrodes.

Each device’s working area is a square 200 nanometers on a side, so more than 20 of them could fit across even a small neuron.

The top electrode is free to move. When the researchers applied a voltage, the two electrodes pulled toward each other and squeezed the film. More current crosses a thinner gap, so the current rose as the film thinned.

Niroui described the film as a “nano-spring” that keeps the metal surfaces from collapsing together for good. From the current, the team calculated that the gap shrank from about 2.3 nanometers to 1.6 nanometers.

They confirmed the squeeze with light. As the voltage rose, light scattered off a device shifted toward red, while a copy built with a stiff ceramic layer instead of PDMS showed no shift.

Peter Satterthwaite, a graduate student who co-led the work with fellow graduate student Sarah Spector, explained why that matters.

“PDMS is viscoelastic, which means that after being compressed, it takes time to return to its original state,” Satterthwaite said.

“This allows the devices to dynamically remember the history of forces and voltages applied to them, and convert that history into an electrical response.”

A pulse lasting 50 milliseconds squeezed the film by about 8 percent, and the current recovered as soon as the voltage stopped. A pulse 10 times longer squeezed it by about 30 percent, and the current returned gradually over several seconds.

So what the device does now depends on what happened to it a few seconds ago. When the team waited only half a second between tests instead of 40 seconds, the film hadn’t fully recovered, and the tests started from a narrower gap.

A neuron in the brain collects incoming signals a little at a time. If they arrive slowly, the charge drains away. If they arrive close together, the charge builds past a threshold, and the neuron fires a signal to its neighbors before resetting.

The neuron device did the same thing. The team sent it a string of 2.5-volt pulses, each too weak to trigger it alone, spaced closer together than the film could recover. After 16 pulses, the current jumped, and the device then relaxed back to where it started.

“We have this complex functionality, which is the basis of biological computing, all contained in one nanoscale device,” he said.

Its memory lasts seconds, while most other artificial neurons hold theirs for millionths or thousandths of a second. The team wrote that this suits tasks that need context over a few seconds.

The researchers also wired two devices to one shared resistor. Once the first device fired, the second couldn’t fire until the first had relaxed, the way one active neuron in a brain can hold back its neighbor.

As built, the device used 54 nanojoules of energy in tests. By the team’s calculation, it only needs to store about 2 femtojoules of electrical energy each time it fires, and a femtojoule is a millionth of a nanojoule.

At 200 nanometers across, the device is more than 100 times smaller than a typical neuron. Cut the current that leaks through it and shrink it further, the team wrote, and it could beat a real neuron on energy efficiency.

The team presented that kind of efficiency as a way to meet the growing demands of artificial intelligence.

“The performance highly relies on the memory introduced using the soft polymer,” Spector said. “We can intentionally engineer this over a large design space to meet the requirements of the desired applications.”

Every measurement was made in a lab, on devices kept under nitrogen gas at 80 percent humidity, and the devices held up better in humid conditions than dry ones. Devices from separate batches behaved alike but not identically.

The team showed single devices and one connected pair, not a network trained to do a task. The authors wrote that practical use will take progress on the materials, the device design and the training methods.

Spector said the material could also suit devices that work with the body, such as prosthetics that process touch quickly or low-power health patches worn on the skin. The team also mentioned robots and environmental sensors.

Next, the team wants to build sensing into the same material, so a single squeezable layer can sense, remember and compute.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

#6392. Scientists figured out how to use a cheap everyday camera to measure how well solar panels work

New digital tools turn massive amounts of complex data into simple, actionable insights to help leaders make better conservation decisions.

Solar panels glow if you run electricity into them in the dark. While photos easily show the bright and dim patches, measuring the exact brightness used to require an expensive, manually calibrated industrial camera.

Jürgen Werner and her research team from the University of Stuttgart, the Research Center Jülich, and the German company Solarzentrum Stuttgart got the same kind of number out of a $450 consumer camera, after writing down how its own electronics respond to light.

The camera is the easy part. A model of how it converts light into numbers is what makes the reading possible, and that model still leans on one reference cell with a known quality.

Push current into a solar cell and it behaves like an LED, giving off light of its own. Silicon cells glow in the infrared range, which the eye can’t see, so the picture has to come from a camera that can.

Engineers already use those pictures to check solar panels for cracked cells and broken connections. What they read is contrast. Bright areas are doing their job, dark ones aren’t.

The brightness itself is a measurement. The fraction of electrons that leave a solar cell as light instead of heat is its luminescent quantum efficiency.

The cell’s open-circuit voltage – the voltage it holds when nothing draws power from it – determines that fraction. Every tenfold rise adds about 60 mV to that voltage.

“An electroluminescence image contains much more quantitative information than simply showing bright and dark regions,” said Werner, of the Institute for Photovoltaics at the University of Stuttgart.

“With a suitable physical camera model and calibration, it can provide absolute luminescent quantum efficiency and, therefore, information about the local quality of a solar cell or module.”

Werner worked with Georgette Udo at Forschungszentrum Jülich and Liviu Stoicescu at Solarzentrum Stuttgart, a German company that inspects photovoltaic systems. Their camera was a Canon EOS 4000D, a low-cost model selling for around €400 in 2026.

Most consumer cameras carry a film over the sensor that absorbs infrared light, so the team took that film out. Astronomy hobbyists make the same change to shoot the night sky.

Then they screwed a long-pass filter onto the lens, which blocks the visible light that would otherwise wash out the faint glow.

The researchers took every photograph in the dark. A current source pushed a known current through each module, and the shutter time, the aperture and the ISO setting decided how much glow reached the sensor.

Brightness was then averaged across a whole cell in ImageJ, free image software, by drawing a box over the cell by hand.

Here is the problem that the model had to solve. A camera doesn’t report light honestly all the way up.

Below a certain brightness the number a pixel returns rises in step with the light that hits it, but above it the pixel fills up and the response stops rising.

That is over-exposure, familiar from any photograph taken into the sun.

Werner’s team measured where their own camera crossed over. It stayed linear below a brightness value of 400, and above that it bent toward a ceiling, which for one module sat at 1,177.

Both stretches are usable once the shape of the curve is known, and the saturated one yields a second estimate of the same quantity.

Converting brightness into quantum efficiency needs an anchor. The team took theirs from a cell with an established efficiency – 1.6 percent at 738 mV – and scaled everything else against it.

Eight silicon modules went under the camera, picked to span decades of production. The oldest was a Solarex panel built in 1978, with a module efficiency of 5.7 percent. At the other end, a Trina module from 2022 reached 21.1 percent.

A modern cell turns far more of its current into light, and by that measure a better cell is simply a brighter one.

Cells in the old panel averaged 560 mV of open-circuit voltage and a luminescent quantum efficiency of 0.0007 percent. Cells in the newer module ran at 687 mV and 0.23 percent.

Across those 45 years the quantum efficiency climbed by roughly a factor of 300.

The model had to fit both ends of that span of solar power manufacturing, and it mostly did. Readings landed where the 60 mV rule predicts, apart from four modules built with multicrystalline solar cells, which trap light less well than single-crystal ones.

Those four only fell into line after the team accounted for the difference.

Werner’s team didn’t put the camera up against an industrial one. The claim is narrower. A model of how a camera turns photons into numbers lets an ordinary one produce absolute values.

The weak points are the ones the authors name themselves. A box drawn by hand over each cell picks up the dark gaps between them, which put scatter in the data. An automatic version still has to be written.

Every measurement was made in the dark, on silicon, on modules whose performance was already known. And the whole scale depends on that single reference cell.

So far the authors haven’t pointed the calibrated camera at a module nobody has measured. That test would show whether the method grades hardware or only confirms what was known.

“Our next step is to use the calibrated camera to determine quantum efficiencies and open-circuit voltages of further, previously uncharacterized solar cells and modules,” Werner said.

He added that the same model should work on a panel lit up rather than powered up, and possibly outdoors.

Daylight matters most. The method needs a dark room, which keeps it in a laboratory. Outdoors, the camera could be carried along a row of panels at a working solar farm.

The full study was published in The Journal of Applied Physics.

#6390. Researchers found a way to grow full size broccoli under solar panels while making electricity at the same time

Under magenta solar panels passing a fraction of the sunlight, broccoli reached full head weight 25 days late while the panels made power.

Placing solar panels over a garden blocks the sun. That normally harms plant growth since most crops require plenty of light. However, that has proven not to be the case under all circumstances.

A new study shows that growing broccoli under special pink solar panels actually helps the plants use sunlight more efficiently.

While it took the broccoli an extra 25 days to mature, they still grew to full size because the semi-transparent panels were designed to let through the best red and blue light for growing.

This setup could allow farmers to harvest both crops and renewable energy from the exact same field.

Silvia Ma Lu of Mälardalen University in Västerås, Sweden, led the work. Her co-authors came from the same University and from two Italian institutes, the Institute for Sustainable Plant Protection in Florence and Università Cattolica in Piacenza.

“The basic concept is quite straightforward,” Ma Lu said. “The solar panels use part of the incoming sunlight to generate renewable electricity while allowing part of the light to pass through to the crops growing underneath.”

A leaf absorbs blue and red light and reflects more of the green, which is why plants look green. A magenta filter does the opposite, passing red and blue and blocking green.

So a magenta solar panel lets through the colors that a crop, such as broccoli, uses and absorbs the rest to make power.

Each panel is a sheet of glass with thin strips of a light-absorbing material, cadmium telluride, spaced across it. A magenta plastic layer inside the glass tints the light that passes between the strips.

Growing crops under panels is called agrivoltaics, and most projects use dark solar panels that cast heavy shade.

Ma Lu’s team built two canopies, each about 13 by 16 feet (4 by 5 meters) and 5 feet (1.5 meters) tall at the low edge.

One used panels the maker rates as 50 percent transparent, the other 70 percent. Under them, broccoli received about 13 and 19 percent, respectively, of the growing light that reached a third, open plot.

Seedlings went into all three plots at Kärrbo Prästgård, a farm in central Sweden, on July 2, 2024. There were thus 44 plants per plot, under white insect netting.

The open-field broccoli was ready to cut after 79 days. At that point the plants growing under the panels were shorter, with smaller heads and thinner stems, so the team let them keep growing.

By day 104, the heads under both canopies weighed about the same as the open-field heads had at day 79. Whole plants in the open still weighed more.

The shaded plants had grown 25 to 41 percent more leaves than their neighbors in the sun. No plant in any plot developed a hollow stem, a defect that the team checked for.

A later harvest could also land in weeks when fresh broccoli sells for more, the authors noted.

Full sun at midday delivered about 925 units of growing light to the open plot, counted as photons per square meter per second.

The canopies passed 143 and 207 of those units, yet the shaded broccoli produced nearly as much plant matter. Each unit of light yielded up to 4.5 times more dry weight than it did in the open.

Single leaves showed the same pattern under a lamp. Leaves from under the panels photosynthesized faster at every light level than leaves from the open plot.

On sunny days the open-field plants were likely getting more light than they could use, Ma Lu’s team wrote. The shaded plants had adjusted to capture more of the little light they did get.

Afternoons under the panels were about 1.8°F (1.0°C) warmer than in the open plot, and nights about 2°F (1.1°C) cooler. The air was also about 6 percent more humid, so the shaded plants lost less water.

Rain was plentiful from September on and, with drip irrigation before that, soil moisture was not what limited either plot.

At the first sampling, iron in the shaded heads was 37 to 41 percent lower than in open-field heads, and manganese was 38 to 42 percent lower. Zinc was down 18 to 20 percent, copper 12 percent, and dissolved sugars by a third to a half.

Calcium, magnesium, and potassium rose instead, 25 to 54 percent higher under the panels in September. By the second harvest those three had fallen back to match the open-field heads, while the four trace metals stayed low.

“One of the most interesting findings was how similarly the broccoli performed under the two solar panel systems despite their different transparency levels,” Ma Lu said.

“However, these findings are specific to our experimental conditions and should be validated across additional growing seasons and system configurations.”

The denser canopy generated an estimated 447.6 kilowatt hours over the season from panels rated at 1.1 kilowatts, converting 7.2 percent of the sunlight hitting them to electricity. Standard silicon panels convert 20 percent or more.

On paper, the team also scaled the numbers up. By that estimate, 2.5 acres (1 hectare) under these panels would produce as much food and power as 2.9 acres (1.18 hectares) split between a field and a solar farm.

“Configurations similar to our prototype may currently be suitable for smaller-scale applications, such as community gardens, or for integration into greenhouse roofs rather than immediate deployment over large agricultural areas,” Ma Lu said.

Each treatment had one plot, six sampled plants, and a single season in central Sweden behind it. Plants at the canopy edges got extra sun and may have shaded or sheltered the ones measured in the middle.

In the 25 days after the open-field harvest, those plants could have grown side shoots for a second cut that the study did not weigh.

The study also can’t separate the magenta color from plain shade or from the softer, scattered light under glass.

Ma Lu’s team has begun testing the magenta panels, along with red and blue ones, under lab lighting where no outside light leaks in.

The full study was published in the journal Cell Reports Physical Science.

#6389. Your voice can now say things you never said

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

AI can replicate a person’s voice. That raises questions about who has the right to use it and what happens when its owner can no longer give consent.

AI technology can create realistic clones of people’s voices. The resulting proliferation of synthetic voices ushers in all sorts of new scenarios, good and bad. “Today, with nothing more than a keyboard and an internet connection, you can type, and you can get an image, a voice, a video of anything, [of] anybody doing or saying anything,” says Hany Farid, a computer scientist at Dartmouth University.

Some of these voice clones are deeply meaningful to people, as in the cases of people who lost their ability to speak. But voice clones can also cause harm, as with scams and deepfakes. And some uses fall into murky gray zones, such as voice clones that “speak” after a person has passed away. What happens to a person’s digital voice after they’re gone?

In this episode of The Deep End: Talk to Me, hear more from Farid, as well as from a former hospital chaplain and AI researcher, and from Jules Rodriguez, a man who communicates with a voice clone. You’ll also hear about a choice Jules made about what will happen to his voice once he’s gone.

Sanders: It’s not clear how these types of interactions might affect grieving. They could help or they could hurt.

Doyle: There is this tension between more healthy continuing bonds. So continuing that relationship by, say, writing letters to your dead loved one or, you know, talking out loud to them and continuing that relationship in a positive way that moves us through a healthy grief process and a grief journey. Or hanging on to our relationship with that person to a degree where we can’t actually do any sort of moving on.

Sanders: Doyle points out that we don’t have good data on how many people might be using griefbots.

Doyle: I just don’t want us to get ahead of ourselves when it comes to people like using these. So the capability to do everything we’ve talked about with griefbots is there. But the actual use cases of individuals in their homes using this, it’s still pretty unclear about the adoption of those technologies.

Sanders: But even if griefbots aren’t widespread, the questions they raise aren’t going away. These voices are blurring the lines between a memory and a present-day experience, between alive and dead. Here’s Karina Nagin again.

Nagin: It’s an interesting conversation that we’re having right now of what happens to your voice once you pass away. Some people are starting to integrate this into their wills or their sort of final wishes of, do you want your voice to be able to speak at your own memorial service?

Do you want to have messages saved in your voice that are for your child at graduation that they listen to? Who and when can use that? I think that these are things that people are starting to think about. Who owns your voice? Can your children use your voice to write a speech for their children’s graduation? Or do you want that voice to be deleted once you pass away? Very tricky questions.

Sanders: Rules about who can use voice clones are all over the place. Regulations vary by state and by country, and even companies have their own individual policies in place. There are no clear guidelines, and that makes sense given how young this technology is. Conversations about digital voices and how to use them are inherently very personal. There are as many different takes as there are people. I asked MA if she and Jules had talked about this.

MA: I love that question. Both of us love this question because it’s so important. And we talked about it before he got the trache. Like when he was already using the voice, we were talking about different things in bed at night. And he said, you know, I have a very clear request that my voice like dies with me, basically, that, you know, I ask that you don’t use the voice to keep me alive in any way,  that there’s no… And I was like, 100 percent clear. I hadn’t even thought about that. But yeah, it would make sense to be like, I miss him so much. I want to, whatever or. But no, as far as we’re concerned, his voice dies when he does. And his voice will live on in whatever videos or things we captured, whatever he’s left us intentionally. And that’s as far as that goes.

Sanders: So when Jules is gone, his voice will be gone too. But right now is a different story.

MA:  Well back in 2021, I was writing an Instagram post about something. It was him playing with Skylar in the backyard while he was already like, you know, had trouble with everything, but he was doing what he could. And I asked him like, you know, what, what do you want to caption it? And he just said that, right here, right now phrase, something else, and like right here, right now. And it became our family mantra. It became something that we wanted to just to share and in both a sense of like do the things that you want to do.

And also something that’s always been big for Jules that I’ve admired him articulate is that it’s not just about, oh, just go forward and do all the things and like suck the marrow out of life. It’s like just also, like, settle. Like it doesn’t have to be that extreme, you know. There’s a beautiful thing about that presence and that settling in. And again, with ALS being something where you’re given the diagnosis, which is terminal, it’s basically a death sentence. Most people are given, you know, two to five years. You don’t know where you’re going to fall in that. We’ve known people that have passed away in a year and a half. We’ve known people that are six years in like Jules, but can still kind of walk around, speak a little bit. ALS touches everybody really differently. So you really don’t know what’s coming. And there’s a lot of like forward thinking that you can do that detaches you from being in your life. So how are you here? And then there’s a lot of backwards, you know, reminiscing and grieving about all the things we’ve lost and how we wish things were different. But then that also takes you out of like this moment right now and this part of your story.

Sanders: This part of the story is the important part. Right here, right now.

On the next and final episode of The Deep End, Talk to Me. We’re going to look at what’s next for Jules and Casey and what’s next for the science racing to give voices back to people.

Vikash Gilja: We can see all the pieces coming together. All of the emphasis, capital, quite frankly, talent focused on advancing AI techniques and technologies. You know, our little corner can benefit from it, right? These tools weren’t available even five years ago.

Sanders: What’s next for the human voice?

Samantha Brosler: Of course, ultimately, we’re hoping to expand this to even larger vocabulary and more range of body movements across the whole body to help allow people more expression in their communication.

This is The Deep End, Talk to Me. I’m Laura Sanders. If you like this podcast tell your friends and leave us a review. It helps the show a lot. Send us your questions and your comments at podcasts@sciencenews.org.
